Docs/Reference

IPC protocol

The Rust daemon owns workspace state. A workspace is a session, a tab is a window, and a pane is a block. Block IDs are also the PTY terminal IDs. Clients render snapshots and issue commands; they must not maintain a competing layout or revision authority. The initial session is default, labeled Workspace. State is in memory and starts fresh on daemon restart.

The payload catalog follows the official Rex event reference. Status parsing follows OSC 7501 revision 0.3, as checked on 2026-10-09. zurafa-events contains the serde payload enums, layout model, snapshot dispatcher, and status record store. Zurafa's version 2 transport envelope below is its own API; it is not Rex's nested CLI envelope. There is no CLI or Lua implementation.

Transport and negotiation

  • Unix socket: $HOME/Library/Application Support/Zurafa/daemon.sock;

    • ZURAFA_SOCKET overrides this, then --socket <path> overrides both.

  • New parent directories use mode 0700; the socket uses mode 0600.
  • Each frame is a four-byte big-endian length followed by UTF-8 JSON, at most

    • 16 MiB. Invalid JSON, non-object messages, oversized frames, or EOF close the connection. A malformed typed request with an ID receives error.

  • First request: { "id": 1, "type": "hello", "protocol": 2 }.

    • Protocol 1 also remains supported. Other first messages receive an error and close. Reply: { "id": 1, "type": "hello_ok", "protocol": 2, "version": "0.1.0" }. No event precedes this reply.

  • Request IDs are unsigned integers. Each valid request gets one reply with its

    • ID. Failures use { "id": 1, "type": "error", "message": "..." }.

  • A second daemon exits successfully if the socket already accepts connections.

    • Disconnecting clients does not stop their PTYs.

PTY operations (both versions)

RequestReply
{id,type:"ping"}{id,type:"pong"}
{id,type:"spawn",cols,rows,cwd?,command?}{id,type:"spawned",terminal}
{id,type:"kill",terminal}{id,type:"ok"}

spawn creates a new window and block in default. Positive cols/rows are u16 values. command is a nonempty string array; omission runs $SHELL (fallback /bin/zsh) with -l. cwd defaults to $HOME. Child environment includes TERM=xterm-256color, COLORTERM=truecolor, and TERM_PROGRAM=Zurafa. A failed spawn makes no layout change. kill terminates the attached child; the retained block is marked stopped when the child is reaped.

Fire-and-forget messages have no reply; malformed ones are ignored:

  • {type:"input",terminal,data:<base64 bytes>}
  • {type:"resize",terminal,cols,rows} — PTY cell dimensions, not split ratios.

Input uses a separate writer thread and a bounded queue of 64 chunks per PTY. Chunks over 1 MiB, or chunks arriving when that queue is full, are dropped. PTY output is broadcast independently of the structured event dispatcher: {type:"output",terminal,data:<base64 bytes>}. OSC 7501 is removed; other terminal bytes pass through. There is no scrollback replay. Slow clients receive {type:"output.gap",missed} when this independent 4096-frame ring overflows; missed counts legacy transport frames, not bytes. Snapshots cannot repair missing screen output.

Protocol 1 additionally receives the legacy {type:"status",terminal,state,message} and {type:"exited",terminal,code} broadcasts without subscribing. done maps to legacy completed; message is decoded text or null. Legacy status messages are a compatibility projection, not the multi-record authority. Protocol 2 uses subscriptions for status and exit events, and receives only PTY byte output on the legacy broadcast path.

Rust-owned layout commands (protocol 2)

Create a tab or split by spawning its PTY:

{"id":10,"type":"layout.tab","session":"default","label":"Shell","cols":80,"rows":24}
{"id":11,"type":"layout.split","session":"default","block":"t1","axis":"horizontal","cols":40,"rows":24}

Both accept optional cwd and command, and reply with spawned. Tab label defaults to Terminal. Axes are horizontal or vertical; the old block is first and the new block second, initially at ratio 0.5. The new block becomes selected, its window becomes active, and splitting clears that window's zoom.

Other changes use {id,type:"layout.command",command:<one of the following>} and reply with ok:

{"op":"focus","session":"default","block":"t1"}
{"op":"zoom","session":"default","block":"t1","enabled":true}
{"op":"resize","session":"default","window":"w1","path":[],"ratio":0.6}
{"op":"close","session":"default","block":"t1"}
{"op":"label","session":"default","window":"w1","label":"Build"}
{"op":"label","session":"default","label":"Work"}
{"op":"create_session","session":"project","label":"Project"}
{"op":"destroy_session","session":"project"}

Remote sessions use the same commands. Add a host with hosts.add, then create a session with that saved host copied into remote:

{"id":30,"type":"hosts.add","host":{"id":"host-1","label":"Build server","hostname":"build.example.net","user":"alice","port":22}}
{"id":31,"type":"hosts.list"}
{"id":32,"type":"layout.command","command":{"op":"create_session","session":"build","label":"Build server","remote":{"id":"host-1","label":"Build server","hostname":"build.example.net","user":"alice","port":22}}}
{"id":33,"type":"hosts.remove","host_id":"host-1"}

hosts.list replies with {id,type:"hosts.list",hosts:[...]}; add/remove reply with ok or error. Saved hosts live in ~/Library/Application Support/Zurafa/hosts.json, written with owner-only permissions. Set ZURAFA_HOSTS_FILE to override the path. A remote session keeps a copy of its host, so removing a saved host does not break an open session. Host changes emit server hosts_changed with an opaque hash. The daemon validates host fields and only accepts a saved host when creating a remote session. Each tab or split in that session runs /usr/bin/ssh -tt -p <port> -- <user@hostname> in a PTY, using the system SSH configuration, keys, known hosts, and authentication prompts. Tailscale DNS names work when the machine can resolve and reach them. There is no separate Tailscale or mosh transport. Sessions are kept in daemon memory; saved host definitions persist across daemon restarts.

A resize path walks a binary split tree (0 = first, 1 = second); [] means the root split. Ratios must be finite and within 0.05–0.95. Focusing a block activates its window, updates selection, and moves existing zoom to that block. Enabling zoom also focuses. Closing a block collapses its split, chooses the first remaining block if necessary, and removes an empty window. If the active window closes, the first remaining window becomes active, or selection is null. Close and session destruction request termination of the removed blocks' PTYs. A removed block no longer emits structured terminal events; kill instead retains it so clients can observe child_exited and its final statuses.

Validation and mutation are serialized. Rejected commands publish nothing and leave state and revisions unchanged. No-op commands also publish nothing. Changes publish their specific events followed by session_view_changed with the new per-session revision. Each successful tab/split/layout change increments that revision once. Terminal reports and exit updates do not change layout revisions. Session creation/destruction publishes server events; a newly created empty session starts at revision 0.

Subscriptions and recovery (protocol 2)

{"id":20,"type":"events.subscribe","subscription":"builds","filter":{"session":"default","category":"terminal","types":["terminal.program_status_changed","terminal.program_status_removed"]}}
{"id":21,"type":"events.subscribe_all","subscription":"everything"}
{"id":22,"type":"events.snapshot"}
{"id":23,"type":"events.resync","subscription":"builds"}
{"id":24,"type":"events.unsubscribe","subscription":"builds"}

Each connection owns up to 64 subscriptions with unique, nonempty IDs of at most 128 bytes. filter defaults to {} (all). Its optional session, block, category (session, terminal, server), and event-name constraints are ANDed. Use types:["terminal.bell","terminal.title_changed"] to select either event: names within types have OR semantics. The existing name string remains supported; if both fields are supplied, name is an additional OR alternative. Omitting both fields (or setting both to null) imposes no name constraint. An explicit types:[] matches no names unless name supplies an alternative. Terminal name filters use terminal.child_exited, etc.; other names are bare. An unknown event name is allowed and currently matches nothing. A server session creation/destruction event can match a session filter; other server events cannot. Block filters select terminal events for that block. Two matching subscriptions intentionally receive separate copies.

Subscribe, subscribe-all, and resync return:

{"id":20,"type":"events.subscribed","subscription":"builds","snapshot":{"protocol":2,"instance":"...","sequence":42,"sessions":{},"clients":{}}}

The snapshot contains all current sessions and clients, independent of the filter. Installing its receiver and copying the snapshot happen under the same lock used for mutations and publication. Events delivered by that subscription have sequence numbers greater than its snapshot watermark. The subscription reply is written before its events. events.snapshot returns the same state shape with reply type events.snapshot; it does not install a subscription. Use subscribe/resync, not separate snapshot + subscribe requests, to establish an atomic boundary.

The snapshot stores session IDs, labels, optional remote host records, revisions, active windows, ordered windows with their binary layouts, selected/zoomed block IDs, and a block map. Each block contains running, nullable exit_code, latest nullable title and pwd, and statuses:{records:{<record id>:<record>}}. Root status ID is "". The clients map contains negotiated live IPC connections. Since this protocol has no client identity negotiation, these use kind:"ipc", name:"IPC client", platform:"unknown", version:"unknown", and principal:null; connected_at is Unix milliseconds. No authenticated identity is inferred.

Structured deliveries look like:

{"type":"events.event","subscription":"builds","event":{"protocol":2,"instance":"...","sequence":43,"timestamp":1790000000000,"category":"terminal","session_id":"default","block_id":"t1","creator_name":"com.superlogical.terminal","type":"block_event","name":"child_exited","payload":{"exit_code":2,"error":"exit status 2"}}}

timestamp is Unix milliseconds; ordering uses the monotonically increasing global sequence, not wall-clock time. Session events carry category, session_id, type, and payload; server events carry category, type, and payload. Terminal events use type:"block_event" and an unqualified name. The daemon instance ID changes on restart, so sequences from different instances are incomparable. Reconnect with a new atomic subscription after restart.

Each subscription has a receiver on the bounded 1024-event Tokio ring. A connection's structured delivery queue is bounded to 128 frames and its request queue to 32. Publishing never waits for a network client. If a receiver lags:

{"type":"events.gap","subscription":"builds","instance":"...","after_sequence":43,"missed":100}

after_sequence is the last global event examined by this subscription, or its snapshot watermark. missed counts overwritten global events, including events that might not have matched its filter. The gap is therefore conservative. A sequence jump in a filtered stream alone is not evidence of loss. Filtered subscription sequence jumps are expected; clients must resync only on events.gap or a daemon-instance change. After a gap the subscription stops until events.resync supplies a fresh snapshot and receiver. Resync retains the filter and discards queued deliveries from the old generation. Unsubscribe aborts the receiver and suppresses its queued deliveries; it replies ok, or error for an unknown subscription. Socket writes preserve per-subscription order; events, replies, and PTY bytes may otherwise interleave.

Typed event payload catalog

The following are serde enums even where their corresponding feature is not implemented. Empty payloads serialize as {}. Unknown added payload fields are ignored on deserialization. Unknown event *variants* are not accepted by these enums; clients should ignore unfamiliar events before typed decoding.

Session eventPayload fieldsEmitted
window_createdwindow_id, labelYes
window_closedwindow_idYes
window_label_changedwindow_id, labelYes
active_window_changedwindow_idYes
block_createdblock_idYes
block_closedblock_idYes
session_label_changedlabelYes
session_view_changedrevisionYes
client_connectedclient_id, principal, connected_atForward type; session attachment unavailable
client_disconnectedclient_id, principalForward type
client_connection_changedclient_id, principal, connection_stateForward type
creator_changedNoneForward type; plugin creators unavailable
Terminal event (terminal. prefix for filters)Payload fieldsSource
child_exitedexit_code, optional errorActual PTY child wait result
pwd_changedpwd, ownerOSC 7 file URL
title_changedtitle, ownerOSC 0 / 2
bellNoneBEL outside OSC
process_changedgeneration, foreground, ancestorsmacOS PTY foreground process group and kernel process metadata
desktop_notificationtitle, bodyOSC 9 or OSC 777 notify
progress_reportstate, progressOSC 9;4 (state 0–4, progress 0–100 or null)
clipboard_writtentextValid UTF-8 base64 OSC 52 write; queries ignored
program_status_changedid, record, reasonValid OSC 7501 report
program_status_removedids, reasonClear, capacity eviction, prompt, reset, child exit

child_exited appears once for a retained block. Successful exit omits error; nonzero exit includes it, and wait failure uses null exit_code plus an error. The reader gets up to 200 ms to drain before exit publication. Descendants may keep the PTY open beyond that deadline, so byte output can continue after exit; subsequent structured reports from that stopped block are ignored. Completed blocks remain in snapshots until closed. Title/pwd owner is null because PTY bytes cannot reliably identify their writing process. The forward owner shape is {pid,name}. Process objects preserve name, cwd, pid, and any additional fields; foreground can be null. On macOS, the daemon samples the PTY foreground process group every 250 ms and publishes a change only when the observed process changes. ancestors is empty until reliable ancestry tracking is implemented. The current process is retained in each block snapshot as foreground, allowing icons to recover after reconnecting. Very short-lived commands may finish between samples; no process identity is guessed from output.

session_createdsession:{session_id,label}Yes

The reference does not specify JSON subtypes for principal or connected_at; the forward types preserve them as JSON values rather than inventing an identity schema. No synthetic events claim unavailable keymaps, hosts, Tailscale, process inspection, or session-client attachment behavior.

OSC 7501 records

Wire syntax is ESC ] 7501 ; key=value (: key=value)* ST, where ST is BEL or ESC \. A feature query with body ? receives the fixed response ESC ] 7501 ; ? ESC \ through the PTY input queue. No report content is sent back to the program. Other observed OSC sequences still reach the terminal renderer; observing clipboard writes does not write to the system clipboard.

Recognized states are idle, working, done, blocked, error, and the removal operation clear. Missing/unknown states are ignored. id omission addresses the root record ("" in snapshots). Reports replace the addressed record completely; missing fields do not inherit values from its old report.

  • msg and title are standard base64 UTF-8, optionally unpadded. Decoded control

    • characters are forbidden. Invalid text rejects the entire report atomically.

  • kind is permission, question, or auth, and applies only to blocked.
  • progress is an integer 0–100 for working/blocked; absent or invalid means

    • indeterminate. It is absent for other states.

  • app is a 1–32 byte token using letters, digits, _ . + -. A record without

    • one resolves the nearest ancestor's app; Records::effective_app implements this dynamically. Snapshots retain only explicitly reported fields.

  • IDs are slash-separated 1–32 byte tokens with the same character set, at most

    • 128 bytes and eight levels. Invalid IDs never fall back to root.

  • clear removes the addressed record and all descendants; root clear removes

    • everything. A nonexistent parent is allowed. Clearing a does not clear ab.

  • Unknown keys and malformed pairs are skipped. Surrounding whitespace is

    • trimmed. The last well-formed duplicate wins, but limit/text validation checks every recognized pair before updating any stored record.

Hard caps: 4096 bytes per complete sequence; keys 16 bytes; msg 2732 encoded / 2048 decoded bytes; title 256 encoded / 192 decoded bytes; 256 records per PTY. New records at capacity evict the least recently updated record. Oversized 7501 sequences are discarded through their terminator with bounded memory, then parsing resumes. Unterminated 7501 sequences are discarded at EOF.

Full reset (ESC c) clears all records. OSC 133 A and attached-child exit remove working and blocked; idle, done, and error survive. Alternate screen changes and soft reset do not affect records. Removal reasons are clear, capacity, reset, shell_prompt, and process_exit; change reason is report. Status events preserve sequence order across fragmented PTY reads. Within a read, byte output is enqueued before its observed reports.

Old Zurafa state=...;message=literal text reports remain accepted with the same text safety and size limits. Legacy completed maps to done. Legacy semicolon syntax is a compatibility extension; new programs should use colon pairs and base64 msg.

Focused validation

Run cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --offline. Tests cover all typed payload variants, combined routing filters, bounded lag and independent subscribers, atomic snapshot boundaries, concurrent publication ordering, layout validation/selection/revisions, status validation/hierarchy/eviction, stream fragmentation, and real PTYs reporting status, title, directory, bell, progress, clipboard text, and notifications. PTY tests also cover feature-query replies, prompt/reset/exit lifetimes, protocol 1 compatibility, protocol 2 snapshots/resync, and fresh daemon instance IDs after restart. Test sockets use relative names inside TMPDIR to stay below macOS Unix socket path limits.
